title: Storage Gateway & Hybrid Storage
summary: Give on-premises apps local access to cloud storage with File, Volume and Tape Gateway.
tldr: **Storage Gateway** runs on premises (VM or hardware appliance, or on EC2) and gives existing apps local protocols (NFS, SMB, iSCSI, VTL) backed by AWS storage, with a local cache for hot data.
Files → **S3 File Gateway** (each file becomes an S3 object). Block → **Volume Gateway**. Tape backups → **Tape Gateway**.
Volume Gateway **cached** keeps the full data set in AWS and only hot data locally; **stored** keeps everything on premises and backs up asynchronously to AWS.

keyFacts.text: **S3 File Gateway** stores files as native S3 objects, so cloud analytics can use the same data while on-prem apps keep their mount.
**Cached volumes**: primary data in AWS, frequently accessed data cached locally. Use it when on-prem capacity can't hold the full data set.
**Stored volumes**: full data set on premises for low latency to everything, with asynchronous point-in-time snapshots to AWS that restore as EBS volumes.
**Tape Gateway** presents a virtual tape library to existing backup software; archived tapes go to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive.
**Amazon FSx File Gateway** is no longer open to new customers. Older questions may still pick it for cached on-prem access to FSx for Windows; new designs use FSx for Windows directly.

traps: Stored volumes keep the full data set on premises, so they don't solve "we can't buy more local storage".
DataSync copies data; it doesn't give apps an ongoing local mount with caching.
Mounting EFS from on premises over VPN works but gives no local cache and isn't for limited-bandwidth sites.
Changing backup jobs to write to an NFS share breaks the "don't change backup procedures" requirement. Tape Gateway keeps them.
S3 File Gateway is not a block device; iSCSI requirements point to Volume Gateway.
